To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
severe protein deficiency and repleton alter body and brain weight, composition and visceral organs in the infant pig.

(1) severe protein deficiency in infant pigs is associated with a reduction in brain weight, (2) protein repletion after 8 wk is sufficient to reverse the effects of 7 wk of severe protein restriction, (3) the response to protein deficiency is similar in obese and lean genetically lean pigs and (4) severe protein deficiency causes atrophy of the small intestine, but repletion for 8 wk is associated with a return to normal architecture.
severe protein deficiency in pigs causes a decrease in body fatness and an increase in fat cell size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of severe protein deficiency on body composition and brain growth.
the effects of protein deficiency and repleton on the body, brain and visceral organs of pigs.
the mechanisms by which protein malnutrition and repletion affect body composition, visceral organ weights and brain development in infant pigs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
severe protein deficiency and refeeding have major effects on body and brain composition in the young growing animal.

protein malnutrition in the young pig causes a severe wasting syndrome, with a loss of body protein and fat, atrophy of the gastrointestinal tract and brain, and a decrease in the weight of all organs, with the exception of the kidney.
severe protein deficiency in young pigs results in a decrease in body fat and protein and an increase in body water.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
severe protein deficiency in the pig results in atrophic gastrointestinal tract and brain, and that these changes are reversible with repletion.
the brain is sensitive to protein deficiency and repleting the protein-deficient infant for 8 wk is not sufficient for the complete restoration of brain cellularity.
severe protein restriction in the infant pig results in atrophic villi in the small intestine, a reduction in absolute cerebrum weight and a decrease in body protein and bone mineral content.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protein deficiency in early life can lead to permanent brain changes that are not reversible by subsequent protein repletion.
the piglet model is a good model for studying human infant nutrition.
the brain of the pig responds to protein deficiency in a way that is similar to that observed in humans.
